title: Chaiti Ghoda: a horse carried by song
lead: A coastal horse dance brings singing, dialogue and community memory together. Follow its performers, a recorded legend and a dated literary-stage encounter.

paragraphs: On 28 September 2013, a horse dance came to IDCOL Auditorium in Bhubaneswar. Sahitya Akademi’s newsletter records a Loka: The Many Voices programme at IDCOL Auditorium, with Guru Utsab Charan Das and his team. The short report names both the performers and the words they were helping to carry.
That is a useful way into Chaiti Ghoda. The horse catches the eye. To understand the performance, leave room for the singer, the reply and the story.

blocks.title: A coastal setting, a portable horse
paragraphs: Odisha Tourism places Chaiti Ghoda among coastal fishing communities. Its introduction describes a dummy horse, elaborate costume, mythological episodes and dialogue made up during the performance. These are clues to a theatrical encounter, rather than a description of people singing as they row.

The Orissa Reference Annual 2009 explains the horse’s construction: a bamboo frame covered with coloured cloth, suspended at the dancer’s waist. The wearer’s movement gives the impression of a rider. The horse has a head, body and tail, but no legs of its own.

blocks.title: Listen to the people around the horse
paragraphs: In the annual’s account, the Rauta leads the singing and commentary. The Rautani, playing his wife, sings and dances alongside him. Dhol and Mohuri accompany them; improvised exchanges and humour enliven the narrative.

For a listener, those roles offer a starting point. Follow a spoken exchange as well as a tune. Notice who begins, who answers, and when movement changes with the music. These are questions to bring to a welcomed performance, not observations from a visit by Project Odisha.

blocks.title: An occasion and a remembered explanation
paragraphs: The 2009 annual connects the dance with Chaitra’s full moon. It also records a legend in which Rama rewards a boatman with a horse after a river crossing. The source presents this as a traditional explanation; it does not establish a founding date.

A legend can explain belonging without providing an archival chronology. Ask how a particular group tells the story and marks the occasion. An old annual’s calendar description cannot confirm the date, route or availability of a performance today.

blocks.title: The words can speak to their own time
paragraphs: The 2013 Sahitya Akademi report adds something to the older description. It credits Utsab Charan Das with writing Chaiti songs addressing subjects including illiteracy, dowry and pollution. Its account shows a named artist bringing contemporary concerns into the repertoire.

This is the organizer’s retrospective report, not a transcript or an evaluation of social change. It does not tell us which verses were performed that evening. But it offers a concrete research path: seek the credited texts and versions, rather than assume the repertoire consists only of inherited mythological stories.

blocks.title: Keep the song with its setting
paragraphs: Chaiti Ghoda’s fishing-community connection makes it a valuable companion to our boat-songs story. It does not make every song in the performance an occupational rowing song. Nor does the horse legend establish a connection with ancient overseas traders. Those histories need their own evidence.

If a group welcomes a conversation, ask which name they use for the form, who made the horse and who taught the songs. Record the singer’s and accompanists’ preferred credits separately. A remembered teacher, a written text and a recent adaptation may belong to different parts of the same account.

Before making or sharing a recording, agree what may be captured and how it may be used. A public appearance does not by itself grant permission to publish a song or an identifiable performer. Sometimes the most useful thing to take home is an accurate name and a better question.

limits: A desk-researched introduction using dated institutional descriptions. Local names, teaching lineages, origin chronology and present-day practice need practitioner-led research. No lyrics, audio, current performance offer or independent human review is claimed.
